### Sequels and other media

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Legend_of_Zelda:_The_Wind_Waker&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Sequels and other media")]

Nintendo initially planned a direct sequel for the GameCube, developed by Aonuma's _Zelda_ team under the working title _Wind Waker 2_. However, _The Wind Waker_'s underwhelming reception in North America, combined with the downturn in the Japanese video game market, convinced Aonuma that the only avenue to success would be a more realistic _Zelda_ game that would appeal to the stronger North American market. He persuaded Miyamoto, who authorized development of a realistically styled game using _The Wind Waker_'s engine, _[Twilight Princess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda:\_Twilight\_Princess "The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess")_, which proved to be a major success for the GameCube and the newly released [Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii "Wii").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Aonuma_2007_1-93)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Aonuma_2007_3-94)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-103)

_The Wind Waker_ originated the variant of the Link character named "[Toon Link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toon_Link "Toon Link")", who appeared in several later Nintendo games.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Fahs-19)_The Wind Waker_ received two direct sequels for the Nintendo DS handheld system. Wanting to continue _The Wind Waker_'s story and art style, in 2007 Aonuma produced _[Phantom Hourglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda:\_Phantom\_Hourglass "The Legend of Zelda: Phantom Hourglass")_, which follows Link and Tetra as they explore new reaches of the Great Sea.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-104)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-105)_[Spirit Tracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda:\_Spirit\_Tracks "The Legend of Zelda: Spirit Tracks")_ (2009) is set roughly a century later and features a new Link and Zelda, the latter a descendent of Tetra, as they traverse New Hyrule with a magical train.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-106)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-107) Toon Link also returned in indirectly related _Legend of Zelda_ games such as _Four Swords Adventures_ (2004), _[The Minish Cap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda:\_The\_Minish\_Cap "The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap")_ (2005), and _[Tri Force Heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda:\_Tri\_Force\_Heroes "The Legend of Zelda: Tri Force Heroes")_ (2015).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Fahs-19)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-108) He also features as a playable character in Nintendo's _[Super Smash Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Smash\_Bros. "Super Smash Bros.")_[crossover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossovers_in_video_games "Crossovers in video games")[fighting game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_game "Fighting game") series, and along with other _Wind Waker_ characters, in the 2016 _Zelda_ pastiche _[Hyrule Warriors Legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyrule\_Warriors\_Legends "Hyrule Warriors Legends")_.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-109)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-110)

Conductors of the concert tour _[The Legend of Zelda: Symphony of the Goddesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda:\_Symphony\_of\_the\_Goddesses "The Legend of Zelda: Symphony of the Goddesses")_ have used custom-made Wind Waker batons.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-111)_The Wind Waker_ also influenced 2017's _[Breath of the Wild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda:\_Breath\_of\_the\_Wild "The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild")_, which features a similarly stylized art design, but with more realistic proportions.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-112)_Breath of the Wild_ also includes species from _The Wind Waker_ among other references, leading some fans to speculate that it follows the "Adult Timeline" established by _The Wind Waker_.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-113)

### Later reputation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Legend_of_Zelda:_The_Wind_Waker&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Later reputation")]

_The Wind Waker_ has continued to be acclaimed by critics. It has appeared in various lists of the [best video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_video_games_considered_the_best "List of video games considered the best"), including those compiled by _Electronic Gaming Monthly_,[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-EGM2006-114)_Nintendo Power_,[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-NintendoPower200-115)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-NintendoPower285-116) and _IGN_.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-ign_top_2006-117)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-IGN_Top_2008-118)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Top_125_Nintendo_Games-119)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-IGN_Top_2015-120)_Nintendo Power_ named _The Wind Waker_ the fourth best game to ever appear on a Nintendo console,[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-NintendoPower200-115) while _[Official Nintendo Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official\_Nintendo\_Magazine "Official Nintendo Magazine")_ placed it 12th.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-121)_Nintendo Power_ listed its ending as one of the greatest in Nintendo history, due to the final battle's climax.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-122)_[UGO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UGO "UGO")_ listed _The Wind Waker_ on their list of the "Top 50 Games That Belong On the 3DS".[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-123) In a retrospective on the GameCube, _IGN_ named _The Wind Waker_ the fourth best game ever released for the system.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-4th-124)_Nintendo Power_ named _The Wind Waker_ the second best GameCube game of all time, behind only _[Resident Evil 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resident\_Evil\_4 "Resident Evil 4")_.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-125)

Later pieces have noted that _The Wind Waker'_ s divisive reputation among fans improved over time and that it has come to be seen as a classic.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-MacDonald-11)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Totilo-91)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Wynne-126)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Gerardi-127)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Drake1-128)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Watts-129) Several writers have said that the game and its stylized aesthetic aged well, whereas contemporary games with more realistic graphics often became dated.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-MacDonald-11)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Drake1-128)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Watts-129) The graphics that initially divided opinion have become a favorite feature;[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Totilo-91)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Gerardi-127) some former skeptics have written about revising their initial opinions.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Wynne-126)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Gerardi-127)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Drake1-128) Nintendo representatives describe this turnaround as a particularly dramatic example of the "Zelda cycle", in which fans' negative responses to _Zelda_ games improve over time.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-Iwata-10) In 2013, Keza MacDonald of _[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")_ wrote that _The Wind Waker_ had outlived its initial reception and become "popularly considered among the very best _Zeldas_".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Waker#cite_note-MacDonald-11)

**Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development Division**,[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-5) commonly abbreviated as **Nintendo EAD** and formerly known as **Nintendo Research & Development No.4 Department**[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-6) (abbreviated as **Nintendo R&D4**), was the largest software development division within the Japanese video game company [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo"). It was preceded by the _Creative Department_, a team of designers with backgrounds in art responsible for many different tasks, to which [Shigeru Miyamoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Miyamoto "Shigeru Miyamoto") and [Takashi Tezuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takashi_Tezuka "Takashi Tezuka") originally belonged.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-7)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-8) Both served as managers of the EARD studios and were credited in every game developed by the division, with varying degrees of involvement. Nintendo EAD was best known for its work on games in the _[Donkey Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Kong "Donkey Kong")_, _[Mario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_(franchise) "Mario (franchise)")_, _[The Legend of Zelda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda "The Legend of Zelda")_, _[F-Zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-Zero "F-Zero")_, _[Star Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Fox "Star Fox")_, _[Animal Crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal\_Crossing "Animal Crossing")_, _[Pikmin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pikmin "Pikmin")_, and _[Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_(video\_game\_series) "Wii (video game series)")_ series.

Following a large company restructuring after the death of company president [Satoru Iwata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoru_Iwata "Satoru Iwata"), the division merged with Nintendo's [Software Planning & Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_Planning_&_Development "Software Planning & Development") division in September 2015, becoming [Nintendo Entertainment Planning & Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Planning_&_Development "Nintendo Entertainment Planning & Development").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Background")]

During the 1970s, when Nintendo was still predominantly a toy company, it decided to expand into [interactive entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interactive_entertainment "Interactive entertainment") and the [video game industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_industry "Video game industry"). Several designers were hired to work under the Creative Department, which, at the time, was the only game development department within Nintendo. Among these new designers were [Makoto Kano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makoto_Kano_(video_game_designer) "Makoto Kano (video game designer)"), who went on to design various [Game & Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_&_Watch "Game & Watch") games, and [Shigeru Miyamoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Miyamoto "Shigeru Miyamoto"), who would create various Nintendo franchises. In 1972, the department was renamed to Research & Development Department; it had about 20 employees. The department was later consolidated into a division and separated into three groups, [Nintendo R&D1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_R&D1 "Nintendo R&D1"), [R&D2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R&D2 "R&D2") and [R&D3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Research_&_Development_3 "Nintendo Research & Development 3").

### 1980–1989: Creation as Research & Development 4

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1980–1989: Creation as Research & Development 4")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Shigeru_Miyamoto_20150610_%28cropped_4%29.jpg/250px-Shigeru_Miyamoto_20150610_%28cropped_4%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shigeru_Miyamoto_20150610_(cropped_4).jpg)

The success of [Shigeru Miyamoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Miyamoto "Shigeru Miyamoto")'s _[Donkey Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Kong\_(arcade\_game) "Donkey Kong (arcade game)")_ arcade game was a deciding factor in the creation of Nintendo R&D4.

Circa 1983, Hiroshi Imanishi oversaw the creation of Research & Development No. 4 Department (commonly abbreviated to Nintendo R&D4), as a new development department dedicated to developing video games for home consoles, complementing the other three existing departments in the [Nintendo Manufacturing Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Manufacturing_Division "Nintendo Manufacturing Division").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-9)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-10)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-11) Imanishi appointed Hiroshi Ikeda, a former director at [Toei Animation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toei_Animation "Toei Animation"), as general manager of the newly created department, and Miyamoto as its chief producer.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-Hiroshi_Ikeda-12) Also hired were [Takashi Tezuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takashi_Tezuka "Takashi Tezuka") and Kenji Miki, graphic designers, Minoru Maeda, a designer, and [Koji Kondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koji_Kondo "Koji Kondo"), [Akito Nakatsuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akito_Nakatsuka "Akito Nakatsuka"), and [Hirokazu Tanaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirokazu_Tanaka "Hirokazu Tanaka"), all sound designers.

Ikeda's creative team had many ideas, but lacked the programming skills to put them into action. _[Mario Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_Bros. "Mario Bros.")_, one of the unit's first games, required assistance in this regard from [Gunpei Yokoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunpei_Yokoi "Gunpei Yokoi") and R&D1. [Toshihiko Nakago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toshihiko_Nakago "Toshihiko Nakago") was familiar with the chipset for the [Family Computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Nintendo Entertainment System"), Nintendo's contemporary home console, as he was originally hired to work with [Masayuki Uemura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masayuki_Uemura "Masayuki Uemura")'s [Nintendo R&D2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_R&D2 "Nintendo R&D2") to develop [software development kits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_development_kit "Software development kit") for Nintendo consoles. When R&D2 and Systems Research and Development, Nakago's company, began porting R&D1-developed arcade games to the Famicom, Shigeru Miyamoto lured him and SRD to R&D4 to help develop _[Excitebike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excitebike "Excitebike")_.

Following the release of _Excitebike_, R&D4 developed a Famicom port of the [beat 'em up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_'em_up "Beat 'em up") arcade game _[Kung-Fu Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kung-Fu\_Master\_(video\_game) "Kung-Fu Master (video game)")_, called _Spartan X_ in Japan and _Kung Fu_ everywhere else. The game improved on features introduced in _Donkey Kong_, representing a key step in the life of the [platform game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platform_game "Platform game") genre.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-Miyamoto_Reveals_All-13)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-14) Their next game was _[Super Mario Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Mario\_Bros. "Super Mario Bros.")_, a self-developed sequel to _Mario Bros._ The game standardized many aspects of the [platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platform_game "Platform game") genre, and went on to be a critical and commercial success. Developed concurrently, but released a year later, was _[The Legend of Zelda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda\_(video\_game) "The Legend of Zelda (video game)")_, an action adventure game. The phenomenal sales of _Mario_ and _Zelda_ made Miyamoto a household name,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-Hiroshi_Ikeda-12) and allowed the department to expand. [Hideki Konno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Konno "Hideki Konno"), [Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi"), [Kensuke Tanabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kensuke_Tanabe "Kensuke Tanabe"), and Takao Shimizu were all hired at this time, and they would become producers themselves.

### 1989–2003: Renamed to Entertainment Analysis & Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1989–2003: Renamed to Entertainment Analysis & Development")]

In 1989, one year before the [Super Famicom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Famicom "Super Famicom") was released in Japan, the R&D4 department was spun-off and made its own division named _Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development_ (commonly abbreviated as _Nintendo EAD_).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-renaming-15) The division was comprised into two departments: the _Software Development Department_, which focused on video game development and was led by Miyamoto, and the Technology Development Department, which focused on programming and developing tools and was led by Takao Sawano.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-16) The technology department relied on R&D2 engineers who assisted SRD with [software libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_libraries "Software libraries"). Following the release of _[F-Zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-Zero\_(video\_game) "F-Zero (video game)")_, the first video game fully programmed by EAD,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-F-Zero_Interview-17) they collaborated with [Argonaut Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argonaut_Software "Argonaut Software") to develop the [Super FX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_FX "Super FX"), a chip which, when placed in Super Famicom cartridges, enabled the use of 3D graphics. As 3D gaming became more prominent, so, too, did the department, programming several of Nintendo EAD's 3D games with SRD.

In 1997, Miyamoto explained that about twenty to thirty employees were devoted to each Nintendo EAD title during the course of its development,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-npinterview-18) and that SRD was a company within the division, formally Nintendo R&D2's software unit, and was composed of about 200 programmers.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-npinterview-18)

In June 2000, in an attempt to include software experts, Nintendo's board of directors invited Miyamoto to join; he also gained responsibility for all of Nintendo's software development, though he would produce further games with EAD.

In 2002, to acquire talent from [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo") who were hesitant to move to Kyoto, Nintendo opened a branch of EAD, appointing Takao Shimizu as manager. Their first project was _[Donkey Kong Jungle Beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Kong\_Jungle\_Beat "Donkey Kong Jungle Beat")_, a [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube") game which made use of the DK Bongos introduced in _[Donkey Konga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Konga "Donkey Konga")_.

### 2004–2015: Restructure, new managers, and merger with SPD

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2004–2015: Restructure, new managers, and merger with SPD")]

In 2004, as a result of a restructuring at Nintendo, several employees at R&D1 and R&D2 were reassigned to EAD, and the department was consolidated into a division, welcoming a new class of managers and producers.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-19)[_[unreliable source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable\_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")_] Tezuka became deputy general manager, and [Eiji Aonuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiji_Aonuma "Eiji Aonuma"), Konno, Shimizu, [Tadashi Sugiyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadashi_Sugiyama "Tadashi Sugiyama"), and [Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi") became producers overseeing their own development teams. Keizo Ota and Yasunari Nishida were appointed project managers of their own groups in the Technology Development Department.

In 2013, Eguchi was promoted to Department Manager of both Software Development Departments in Kyoto and Tokyo. As such, he left his role as Group Manager of _Software Development Group No. 2_, and was replaced by [Hisashi Nogami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hisashi_Nogami "Hisashi Nogami"). On June 18, 2014, the EAD Kyoto branch was moved from the Nintendo Central Office to the _Nintendo Development Center_ in Kyoto. The building housed more than 1100 developers from all of Nintendo's internal research and development divisions, which included the Nintendo EAD, [SPD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Software_Planning_&_Development "Nintendo Software Planning & Development"), [IRD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Integrated_Research_&_Development "Nintendo Integrated Research & Development") and [SDD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_System_Development "Nintendo System Development") divisions.

On September 16, 2015, during a restructuring overshadowed by the recent death of president [Satoru Iwata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoru_Iwata "Satoru Iwata"), EAD merged with [Nintendo Software Planning & Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Software_Planning_&_Development "Nintendo Software Planning & Development"), forming [Entertainment Planning & Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Planning_&_Development "Entertainment Planning & Development") (EPD).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-20)

The Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development division was headed by Nintendo-veteran [Takashi Tezuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takashi_Tezuka "Takashi Tezuka") who acted as general manager. The division was divided in two development departments: one in Kyoto, with [Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi") acting as its deputy general manager; and one in Tokyo, with [Yoshiaki Koizumi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoshiaki_Koizumi "Yoshiaki Koizumi") acting as its deputy general manager.

### Kyoto Software Development Department

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Kyoto Software Development Department")]

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8d/Katsuya_Eguchi_at_E3_2012_Nintendo_Conference_%28edited%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Katsuya_Eguchi_at_E3_2012_Nintendo_Conference_(edited).jpg)

[Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi"), Deputy General Manager of the Nintendo EAD division in Kyoto

The Nintendo EAD Kyoto _Software Development Department_ was the largest and one of the oldest research and development departments within Nintendo, housing more than 700 video game developers. It was located in [Kyoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto "Kyoto"), Japan, formerly in the _Nintendo Central Office_, but on June 28, 2014, it was relocated to the new _Nintendo Development Center_, which housed all of Nintendo's internal research and development divisions.

The development department integrated Nintendo's most notable producers: [Hideki Konno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Konno "Hideki Konno"), producer of the _[Nintendogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendogs "Nintendogs")_ and _[Mario Kart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_Kart "Mario Kart")_ series; [Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi"), producer of the _[Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_(series) "Wii (series)")_ and _[Animal Crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal\_Crossing "Animal Crossing")_ series; [Eiji Aonuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiji_Aonuma "Eiji Aonuma"), producer of _[The Legend of Zelda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda "The Legend of Zelda")_ series; [Hiroyuki Kimura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroyuki_Kimura "Hiroyuki Kimura"), producer of the _[Big Brain Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big\_Brain\_Academy "Big Brain Academy")_, _[Super Mario Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Mario\_Bros. "Super Mario Bros.")_, and _[Pikmin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pikmin "Pikmin")_ series; and [Tadashi Sugiyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadashi_Sugiyama "Tadashi Sugiyama"), producer of the _[Wii Fit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_Fit "Wii Fit")_, _[Steel Diver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel\_Diver "Steel Diver")_ and _[Star Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Fox "Star Fox")_ series.

The department was managed by veteran Nintendo game designer [Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi"). As such, [Hisashi Nogami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hisashi_Nogami "Hisashi Nogami") later succeeded him as the producer of the _[Animal Crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal\_Crossing "Animal Crossing")_ franchise and was responsible for the creation of the _[Splatoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splatoon "Splatoon")_ series.

### Tokyo Software Development Department

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tokyo Software Development Department")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Yoshiaki_Koizumi_2007.jpg/250px-Yoshiaki_Koizumi_2007.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yoshiaki_Koizumi_2007.jpg)

[Yoshiaki Koizumi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoshiaki_Koizumi "Yoshiaki Koizumi") became manager of a second department of the Nintendo EAD division in Tokyo after 2007.

The Nintendo EAD _Tokyo Software Development Department_ was created in 2002 with the goal of bringing in fresh new talent from the capital of Japan who wouldn't be willing to travel hundreds of miles away to Kyoto. It is located in [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo"), Japan, in the Nintendo Tokyo Office.

In 2003, twenty members of the Entertainment Analysis & Development Division in Kyoto volunteered to relocate to Nintendo's Tokyo Office to expand development resources. These twenty volunteers were primarily from the _Super Mario Sunshine_ team. Management saw it as a good opportunity to expand and recruit several developers who were more comfortable living in Tokyo than relocating to Kyoto.

Takao Shimizu (original manager and producer) and [Yoshiaki Koizumi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoshiaki_Koizumi "Yoshiaki Koizumi") (director) began hiring several recruits in Tokyo coming from several established companies like SEGA, Koei, and Square-Enix. Shimizu and Koizumi jointly spearheaded their first project, _Donkey Kong Jungle Beat_. This was followed in 2007 by the release of the critically and commercially acclaimed _Super Mario Galaxy_. After the release of _Super Mario Galaxy_, Koizumi was promoted to manager and producer and officially opened Tokyo Software Development Group No. 2.

The Tokyo group had veteran game developer [Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi") as its general manager, who also oversaw development operations for the Kyoto Software Development Department.

**Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development Division**,[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-5) commonly abbreviated as **Nintendo EAD** and formerly known as **Nintendo Research & Development No.4 Department**[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-6) (abbreviated as **Nintendo R&D4**), was the largest software development division within the Japanese video game company [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo"). It was preceded by the _Creative Department_, a team of designers with backgrounds in art responsible for many different tasks, to which [Shigeru Miyamoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Miyamoto "Shigeru Miyamoto") and [Takashi Tezuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takashi_Tezuka "Takashi Tezuka") originally belonged.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-7)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-8) Both served as managers of the EARD studios and were credited in every game developed by the division, with varying degrees of involvement. Nintendo EAD was best known for its work on games in the _[Donkey Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Kong "Donkey Kong")_, _[Mario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_(franchise) "Mario (franchise)")_, _[The Legend of Zelda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda "The Legend of Zelda")_, _[F-Zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-Zero "F-Zero")_, _[Star Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Fox "Star Fox")_, _[Animal Crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal\_Crossing "Animal Crossing")_, _[Pikmin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pikmin "Pikmin")_, and _[Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_(video\_game\_series) "Wii (video game series)")_ series.

Following a large company restructuring after the death of company president [Satoru Iwata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoru_Iwata "Satoru Iwata"), the division merged with Nintendo's [Software Planning & Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_Planning_&_Development "Software Planning & Development") division in September 2015, becoming [Nintendo Entertainment Planning & Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Planning_&_Development "Nintendo Entertainment Planning & Development").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Background")]

During the 1970s, when Nintendo was still predominantly a toy company, it decided to expand into [interactive entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interactive_entertainment "Interactive entertainment") and the [video game industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_industry "Video game industry"). Several designers were hired to work under the Creative Department, which, at the time, was the only game development department within Nintendo. Among these new designers were [Makoto Kano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makoto_Kano_(video_game_designer) "Makoto Kano (video game designer)"), who went on to design various [Game & Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_&_Watch "Game & Watch") games, and [Shigeru Miyamoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Miyamoto "Shigeru Miyamoto"), who would create various Nintendo franchises. In 1972, the department was renamed to Research & Development Department; it had about 20 employees. The department was later consolidated into a division and separated into three groups, [Nintendo R&D1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_R&D1 "Nintendo R&D1"), [R&D2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R&D2 "R&D2") and [R&D3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Research_&_Development_3 "Nintendo Research & Development 3").

### 1980–1989: Creation as Research & Development 4

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1980–1989: Creation as Research & Development 4")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Shigeru_Miyamoto_20150610_%28cropped_4%29.jpg/250px-Shigeru_Miyamoto_20150610_%28cropped_4%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Shigeru_Miyamoto_20150610_(cropped_4).jpg)

The success of [Shigeru Miyamoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shigeru_Miyamoto "Shigeru Miyamoto")'s _[Donkey Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Kong\_(arcade\_game) "Donkey Kong (arcade game)")_ arcade game was a deciding factor in the creation of Nintendo R&D4.

Circa 1983, Hiroshi Imanishi oversaw the creation of Research & Development No. 4 Department (commonly abbreviated to Nintendo R&D4), as a new development department dedicated to developing video games for home consoles, complementing the other three existing departments in the [Nintendo Manufacturing Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Manufacturing_Division "Nintendo Manufacturing Division").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-9)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-10)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-11) Imanishi appointed Hiroshi Ikeda, a former director at [Toei Animation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toei_Animation "Toei Animation"), as general manager of the newly created department, and Miyamoto as its chief producer.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-Hiroshi_Ikeda-12) Also hired were [Takashi Tezuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takashi_Tezuka "Takashi Tezuka") and Kenji Miki, graphic designers, Minoru Maeda, a designer, and [Koji Kondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koji_Kondo "Koji Kondo"), [Akito Nakatsuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akito_Nakatsuka "Akito Nakatsuka"), and [Hirokazu Tanaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirokazu_Tanaka "Hirokazu Tanaka"), all sound designers.

Ikeda's creative team had many ideas, but lacked the programming skills to put them into action. _[Mario Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_Bros. "Mario Bros.")_, one of the unit's first games, required assistance in this regard from [Gunpei Yokoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunpei_Yokoi "Gunpei Yokoi") and R&D1. [Toshihiko Nakago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toshihiko_Nakago "Toshihiko Nakago") was familiar with the chipset for the [Family Computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Nintendo Entertainment System"), Nintendo's contemporary home console, as he was originally hired to work with [Masayuki Uemura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masayuki_Uemura "Masayuki Uemura")'s [Nintendo R&D2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_R&D2 "Nintendo R&D2") to develop [software development kits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_development_kit "Software development kit") for Nintendo consoles. When R&D2 and Systems Research and Development, Nakago's company, began porting R&D1-developed arcade games to the Famicom, Shigeru Miyamoto lured him and SRD to R&D4 to help develop _[Excitebike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excitebike "Excitebike")_.

Following the release of _Excitebike_, R&D4 developed a Famicom port of the [beat 'em up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_'em_up "Beat 'em up") arcade game _[Kung-Fu Master](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kung-Fu\_Master\_(video\_game) "Kung-Fu Master (video game)")_, called _Spartan X_ in Japan and _Kung Fu_ everywhere else. The game improved on features introduced in _Donkey Kong_, representing a key step in the life of the [platform game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platform_game "Platform game") genre.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-Miyamoto_Reveals_All-13)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-14) Their next game was _[Super Mario Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Mario\_Bros. "Super Mario Bros.")_, a self-developed sequel to _Mario Bros._ The game standardized many aspects of the [platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platform_game "Platform game") genre, and went on to be a critical and commercial success. Developed concurrently, but released a year later, was _[The Legend of Zelda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda\_(video\_game) "The Legend of Zelda (video game)")_, an action adventure game. The phenomenal sales of _Mario_ and _Zelda_ made Miyamoto a household name,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-Hiroshi_Ikeda-12) and allowed the department to expand. [Hideki Konno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Konno "Hideki Konno"), [Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi"), [Kensuke Tanabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kensuke_Tanabe "Kensuke Tanabe"), and Takao Shimizu were all hired at this time, and they would become producers themselves.

### 1989–2003: Renamed to Entertainment Analysis & Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1989–2003: Renamed to Entertainment Analysis & Development")]

In 1989, one year before the [Super Famicom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Famicom "Super Famicom") was released in Japan, the R&D4 department was spun-off and made its own division named _Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development_ (commonly abbreviated as _Nintendo EAD_).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-renaming-15) The division was comprised into two departments: the _Software Development Department_, which focused on video game development and was led by Miyamoto, and the Technology Development Department, which focused on programming and developing tools and was led by Takao Sawano.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-16) The technology department relied on R&D2 engineers who assisted SRD with [software libraries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_libraries "Software libraries"). Following the release of _[F-Zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-Zero\_(video\_game) "F-Zero (video game)")_, the first video game fully programmed by EAD,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-F-Zero_Interview-17) they collaborated with [Argonaut Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argonaut_Software "Argonaut Software") to develop the [Super FX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_FX "Super FX"), a chip which, when placed in Super Famicom cartridges, enabled the use of 3D graphics. As 3D gaming became more prominent, so, too, did the department, programming several of Nintendo EAD's 3D games with SRD.

In 1997, Miyamoto explained that about twenty to thirty employees were devoted to each Nintendo EAD title during the course of its development,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-npinterview-18) and that SRD was a company within the division, formally Nintendo R&D2's software unit, and was composed of about 200 programmers.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-npinterview-18)

In June 2000, in an attempt to include software experts, Nintendo's board of directors invited Miyamoto to join; he also gained responsibility for all of Nintendo's software development, though he would produce further games with EAD.

In 2002, to acquire talent from [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo") who were hesitant to move to Kyoto, Nintendo opened a branch of EAD, appointing Takao Shimizu as manager. Their first project was _[Donkey Kong Jungle Beat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Kong\_Jungle\_Beat "Donkey Kong Jungle Beat")_, a [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube") game which made use of the DK Bongos introduced in _[Donkey Konga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donkey\_Konga "Donkey Konga")_.

### 2004–2015: Restructure, new managers, and merger with SPD

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2004–2015: Restructure, new managers, and merger with SPD")]

In 2004, as a result of a restructuring at Nintendo, several employees at R&D1 and R&D2 were reassigned to EAD, and the department was consolidated into a division, welcoming a new class of managers and producers.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-19)[_[unreliable source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable\_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")_] Tezuka became deputy general manager, and [Eiji Aonuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiji_Aonuma "Eiji Aonuma"), Konno, Shimizu, [Tadashi Sugiyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadashi_Sugiyama "Tadashi Sugiyama"), and [Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi") became producers overseeing their own development teams. Keizo Ota and Yasunari Nishida were appointed project managers of their own groups in the Technology Development Department.

In 2013, Eguchi was promoted to Department Manager of both Software Development Departments in Kyoto and Tokyo. As such, he left his role as Group Manager of _Software Development Group No. 2_, and was replaced by [Hisashi Nogami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hisashi_Nogami "Hisashi Nogami"). On June 18, 2014, the EAD Kyoto branch was moved from the Nintendo Central Office to the _Nintendo Development Center_ in Kyoto. The building housed more than 1100 developers from all of Nintendo's internal research and development divisions, which included the Nintendo EAD, [SPD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Software_Planning_&_Development "Nintendo Software Planning & Development"), [IRD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Integrated_Research_&_Development "Nintendo Integrated Research & Development") and [SDD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_System_Development "Nintendo System Development") divisions.

On September 16, 2015, during a restructuring overshadowed by the recent death of president [Satoru Iwata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoru_Iwata "Satoru Iwata"), EAD merged with [Nintendo Software Planning & Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Software_Planning_&_Development "Nintendo Software Planning & Development"), forming [Entertainment Planning & Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Planning_&_Development "Entertainment Planning & Development") (EPD).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_&_Development#cite_note-20)

The Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development division was headed by Nintendo-veteran [Takashi Tezuka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Takashi_Tezuka "Takashi Tezuka") who acted as general manager. The division was divided in two development departments: one in Kyoto, with [Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi") acting as its deputy general manager; and one in Tokyo, with [Yoshiaki Koizumi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoshiaki_Koizumi "Yoshiaki Koizumi") acting as its deputy general manager.

### Kyoto Software Development Department

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Kyoto Software Development Department")]

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8d/Katsuya_Eguchi_at_E3_2012_Nintendo_Conference_%28edited%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Katsuya_Eguchi_at_E3_2012_Nintendo_Conference_(edited).jpg)

[Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi"), Deputy General Manager of the Nintendo EAD division in Kyoto

The Nintendo EAD Kyoto _Software Development Department_ was the largest and one of the oldest research and development departments within Nintendo, housing more than 700 video game developers. It was located in [Kyoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto "Kyoto"), Japan, formerly in the _Nintendo Central Office_, but on June 28, 2014, it was relocated to the new _Nintendo Development Center_, which housed all of Nintendo's internal research and development divisions.

The development department integrated Nintendo's most notable producers: [Hideki Konno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hideki_Konno "Hideki Konno"), producer of the _[Nintendogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendogs "Nintendogs")_ and _[Mario Kart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_Kart "Mario Kart")_ series; [Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi"), producer of the _[Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_(series) "Wii (series)")_ and _[Animal Crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal\_Crossing "Animal Crossing")_ series; [Eiji Aonuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiji_Aonuma "Eiji Aonuma"), producer of _[The Legend of Zelda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Legend\_of\_Zelda "The Legend of Zelda")_ series; [Hiroyuki Kimura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroyuki_Kimura "Hiroyuki Kimura"), producer of the _[Big Brain Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big\_Brain\_Academy "Big Brain Academy")_, _[Super Mario Bros.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super\_Mario\_Bros. "Super Mario Bros.")_, and _[Pikmin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pikmin "Pikmin")_ series; and [Tadashi Sugiyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadashi_Sugiyama "Tadashi Sugiyama"), producer of the _[Wii Fit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii\_Fit "Wii Fit")_, _[Steel Diver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel\_Diver "Steel Diver")_ and _[Star Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Fox "Star Fox")_ series.

The department was managed by veteran Nintendo game designer [Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi"). As such, [Hisashi Nogami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hisashi_Nogami "Hisashi Nogami") later succeeded him as the producer of the _[Animal Crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal\_Crossing "Animal Crossing")_ franchise and was responsible for the creation of the _[Splatoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splatoon "Splatoon")_ series.

### Tokyo Software Development Department

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nintendo_Entertainment_Analysis_%26_Development&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tokyo Software Development Department")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Yoshiaki_Koizumi_2007.jpg/250px-Yoshiaki_Koizumi_2007.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yoshiaki_Koizumi_2007.jpg)

[Yoshiaki Koizumi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoshiaki_Koizumi "Yoshiaki Koizumi") became manager of a second department of the Nintendo EAD division in Tokyo after 2007.

The Nintendo EAD _Tokyo Software Development Department_ was created in 2002 with the goal of bringing in fresh new talent from the capital of Japan who wouldn't be willing to travel hundreds of miles away to Kyoto. It is located in [Tokyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo "Tokyo"), Japan, in the Nintendo Tokyo Office.

In 2003, twenty members of the Entertainment Analysis & Development Division in Kyoto volunteered to relocate to Nintendo's Tokyo Office to expand development resources. These twenty volunteers were primarily from the _Super Mario Sunshine_ team. Management saw it as a good opportunity to expand and recruit several developers who were more comfortable living in Tokyo than relocating to Kyoto.

Takao Shimizu (original manager and producer) and [Yoshiaki Koizumi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoshiaki_Koizumi "Yoshiaki Koizumi") (director) began hiring several recruits in Tokyo coming from several established companies like SEGA, Koei, and Square-Enix. Shimizu and Koizumi jointly spearheaded their first project, _Donkey Kong Jungle Beat_. This was followed in 2007 by the release of the critically and commercially acclaimed _Super Mario Galaxy_. After the release of _Super Mario Galaxy_, Koizumi was promoted to manager and producer and officially opened Tokyo Software Development Group No. 2.

The Tokyo group had veteran game developer [Katsuya Eguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsuya_Eguchi "Katsuya Eguchi") as its general manager, who also oversaw development operations for the Kyoto Software Development Department.

_**Pokémon Ruby Version**_[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-1) and _**Pokémon Sapphire Version**_[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-2) are 2002[role-playing video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Role-playing_video_game "Role-playing video game") developed by [Game Freak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Freak "Game Freak") and published by [The Pokémon Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pok%C3%A9mon_Company "The Pokémon Company") and [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") for the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance"). They are the first installments in the third generation of the [_Pokémon_ video game series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_(video_game_series) "Pokémon (video game series)"), also known as the "advanced generation". After years of Nintendo being the sole publisher of the franchise in all regions, The Pokémon Company co-published the games for the first time since the establishment of the joint-owned company in 1998. They were first released in Japan in late 2002, and internationally in 2003. _[Pokémon Emerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Emerald "Pokémon Emerald")_, a third version, was released two years later in each region. [Remakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_remake "Video game remake") of the two games, titled [_Pokémon Omega Ruby_ and _Alpha Sapphire_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Omega_Ruby_and_Alpha_Sapphire "Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire"), were released for the [Nintendo 3DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_3DS "Nintendo 3DS") worldwide in November 2014, exactly twelve years to the date of the original _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ release date, with the exception of Europe, where it released a week later.

The gameplay is mostly unchanged from the previous games; the player controls the main character from an [overhead perspective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhead_perspective "Overhead perspective"), and the controls are largely the same as those of previous games. As with previous games, the main objectives are to catch all of the Pokémon in the games and defeat the [Elite Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elite_Four "Elite Four") and the Pokémon League Champion; also like their predecessors, the games' main subplot involves the player character defeating a criminal organization that attempts to take over the region. New features, such as double battles, [Pokémon abilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_abilities "Pokémon abilities"), Pokémon Contests, and 135 new Pokémon were added.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-3)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-5) Owing to the increased capabilities of the Game Boy Advance, four players may be [connected to each other](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance_Game_Link_Cable "Game Boy Advance Game Link Cable") at a time instead of the previous limit of two. Additionally, the games can be connected to an [e-Reader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_e-Reader "Nintendo e-Reader") or other third-generation _Pokémon_ games.

_Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ received mostly positive reviews; praise was given to the new features and Pokémon designs, though critics were divided in their assessment of the games, especially on the gameplay and graphics. Most of the complaints focused on gameplay not changing much in relation to previous generations. With over 16.22 million copies sold, they were a commercial success and became the [best-selling game for the Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_Game_Boy_Advance_video_games "List of best-selling Game Boy Advance video games"); however, the games sold less than previous generations with _Red_ and _Blue_ having sold nearly 31 million units worldwide, and _Gold_ and _Silver_ selling over 23.10 million units.

## Gameplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Gameplay")]

See also: [Gameplay of _Pokémon_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gameplay_of_Pok%C3%A9mon "Gameplay of Pokémon")

The basic mechanics of _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ are largely the same as their predecessors. As with all _Pokémon_ games for [handheld consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handheld_console "Handheld console"), the gameplay is in [third-person](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third-person_(video_games) "Third-person (video games)"), overhead perspective and consists of three basic screens: a [field map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overworld "Overworld"), in which the player navigates the main character; a battle screen; and the menu, in which the player configures their party, items, or gameplay settings. Players begin the game with one Pokémon and can capture more using [Poké Balls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9_Ball "Poké Ball"). They can also use their Pokémon to battle other Pokémon. When the player [encounters a wild Pokémon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_encounter "Random encounter") or is challenged by a trainer to a battle, the screen switches to a [turn-based](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn-based "Turn-based") battle screen where the Pokémon fight.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-6) During a battle, the player may [use a move](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gameplay_of_Pok%C3%A9mon#Pok%C3%A9mon_moves "Gameplay of Pokémon"), use an item, switch their active Pokémon, or flee, although fleeing is not an option in battles against trainers. All Pokémon have [hit points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit_points "Hit points") (HP); when a Pokémon's HP is reduced to zero, it faints and cannot battle until it is revived. If the player's Pokémon defeats the opposing Pokémon (causes it to faint), it receives [experience points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_points "Experience points"). After accumulating enough experience points, it will [level up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_point#Level-based_progression "Experience point"); most Pokémon [evolve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_evolution "Pokémon evolution") into a new species of Pokémon when they reach a certain level.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-7)

Apart from battling, capturing Pokémon is the most essential element of _Pokémon_ gameplay. During a battle with a wild Pokémon, the player may use a Poké Ball on them. If successful, the Pokémon will be added to the player's active party, or stored if the player already has the maximum six Pokémon in their party.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-8) Factors in the success rate of capture include the HP, status effects such as Paralysis or Sleep, and the strength of the Poké Ball used: the lower the target's HP and the stronger the Poké Ball, the higher the success rate of capture is.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-9) Other trainers' Pokémon cannot be captured.

### New features

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: New features")]

See also: [List of generation III Pokémon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_generation_III_Pok%C3%A9mon "List of generation III Pokémon")

The most prominent change in the battle mechanics is the introduction of double battles, in which the opposing parties each use two Pokémon at the same time. Consequently, certain [Pokémon moves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_moves "Pokémon moves") can affect multiple combatants at once.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-10) Multi battles were added alongside double battles. They are identical to double battles, but there are two trainers to a side, each controlling one of the two Pokémon sent out. Also new to the games are [innate abilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_abilities "Pokémon abilities") and [natures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_natures "Pokémon natures"); the former is shared by every Pokémon of a certain species, while the latter may vary among a particular species. Abilities grant their holders certain powers in battle, such as immunity against certain [types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_types "Pokémon types") of moves or strengthening a certain type of move. Natures, like innate abilities, affect the strength of Pokémon in battle; however, they affect the stats of the Pokémon rather than directly affecting the strength of the moves.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-11) Another stat introduced in _Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ is Condition, an important factor in Pokémon Contests, mini-games in which participants perform moves before a judge. Both Pokémon and their moves have a Condition, which is increased by using Pokéblocks, which are candies made from berries.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-12) Secret bases were added as a one-off feature where players could open up a hole in the world and customize the area with various items picked up in-game. Players who linked up with others who set up secret bases were able to battle an [NPC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-player_character "Non-player character") version of that trainer within their secret base.

Like [_Pokémon Gold_, _Silver_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Gold_and_Silver "Pokémon Gold and Silver"), and _[Crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Crystal "Pokémon Crystal")_, _Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ keep track of real-life time; this influences events like tides and berry plant growth. However, unlike their predecessors, _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ do not differentiate between day and night. Also, due to the differences in the technical specifications of Game Boy link cables and Game Boy Advance link cables, _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ cannot be linked with Pokémon games of previous generations; one cannot battle with or trade with the previous generations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-13)

### Connectivity to other devices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Connectivity to other devices")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Eon_Ticket.jpg/250px-Eon_Ticket.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eon_Ticket.jpg)

The Eon Ticket could be scanned in by the [e-Reader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_e-Reader "Nintendo e-Reader") to go and catch either [Latios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latios "Latios") or [Latias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latias "Latias"), depending on the game.

_Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ have limited [e-Reader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_e-Reader "Nintendo e-Reader") support. Nintendo released Battle-e Cards, a set of e-Reader cards that contained trainer battles in which the player could see previously hidden Pokémon.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-14) A special e-Reader card called the Eon Ticket was also released; obtained through the Mystery Gift function, the Ticket allows the player to reach a place called Southern Island. There, the player faces either [Latios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latios "Latios") or [Latias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latias "Latias"), depending on which version of the game is used.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-eonticket-15)

_Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ are also able to connect to the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube") games _[Pokémon Colosseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Colosseum "Pokémon Colosseum")_, _[Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_XD:\_Gale\_of\_Darkness "Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness")_ and _[Pokémon Box: Ruby and Sapphire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Box:\_Ruby\_and\_Sapphire "Pokémon Box: Ruby and Sapphire")_. In the former two, once players reach a certain point in the game, they are able to transfer Pokémon between _Colosseum_ / _XD_ and _Ruby_ / _Sapphire_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-16) Additionally, those who pre-ordered _Colosseum_ were able to access the Pokémon [Jirachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jirachi "Jirachi") and see a preview of the movie _[Pokémon: Jirachi Wish Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon:\_Jirachi\_Wish\_Maker "Pokémon: Jirachi Wish Maker")_. _Pokémon Box_ allows players to store and organize their Pokémon on the GameCube.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-17) Also, in the European version of _[Pokémon Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Channel "Pokémon Channel")_, players could receive a Jirachi at a certain point in the game, which they could then transfer over to _Ruby_ or _Sapphire_.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Plot")]

### Setting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Setting")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/7/75/Hoenn_%28map%29.jpg/250px-Hoenn_%28map%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hoenn_(map).jpg)

_Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ are set in the Hoenn Region, designed to be similar to Japan's island of Kyushu if rotated 90°. (pictured below).

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Kyushu_relief_map.svg/250px-Kyushu_relief_map.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kyushu_relief_map.svg)

[Kyushu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyushu "Kyushu") island, Japan

_Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ occur in the Hoenn Region, some distance from the Kanto and Johto Regions featured in previous games. The design of Hoenn was based on the Japanese island and region of [Kyushu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyushu "Kyushu"); however, Hoenn is rotated 90° relative to Kyushu, as [Junichi Masuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junichi_Masuda "Junichi Masuda") felt that it would provide a better gameplay balance.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-hiddenpower-18) Like Kyushu, Hoenn possesses many smaller islands, and part of the region is dominated by sea routes, several of which contain areas where the player can dive underwater.

### Story

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Story")]

See also: [List of _Pokémon_ characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pok%C3%A9mon_characters "List of Pokémon characters") and [List of Pokémon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pok%C3%A9mon "List of Pokémon")

Like other _Pokémon_ games, _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_'s gameplay is [linear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_gameplay "Linear gameplay"); the main events occur in a fixed order.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-19) The [protagonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protagonist "Protagonist") of _Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ are Brendan and May, who have recently moved to a small town called Littleroot Town. At the beginning of the games, the player chooses either [Treecko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treecko "Treecko"), [Torchic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torchic "Torchic"), or [Mudkip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudkip "Mudkip") to protect Professor Birch, the regional professor, from attacking [Poochyena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poochyena "Poochyena"). After defending Birch, the player is taken to his lab and receives the chosen Pokémon as their [starter Pokémon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starter_Pok%C3%A9mon "Starter Pokémon"). After that, the player encounters May/Brendan, the child of Professor Birch. The player's rival, who appears as the professor's child, is also a [Pokémon Trainer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trainer "Pokémon Trainer") and occasionally battles the player.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-20) The games' two main goals are defeating the eight Gym Leaders, proving oneself worthy of challenging the Elite Four and Hoenn League Champion to become the new Hoenn League Champion and completing the [Pokédex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9dex "Pokédex") by capturing, evolving, and trading to obtain all 202 Pokémon available between _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_. It is possible to obtain all 386 Pokémon, but this requires trading with [_Pokémon FireRed_ and _LeafGreen_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_FireRed_and_LeafGreen "Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen") or _[Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_XD:\_Gale\_of\_Darkness "Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness")_ and _[Pokémon Colosseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Colosseum "Pokémon Colosseum")_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-21)

In addition to the main quest of defeating the Gym Leaders, there are side quests in which the player can aid NPCs by fulfilling tasks, usually by obtaining items. The most prominent subplot involves [Team Aqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_Aqua "Team Aqua") and [Team Magma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_Magma "Team Magma"), crime syndicates who want to use Pokémon to alter the climate of Hoenn: in _Ruby_, the villains, Team Magma, want to use the legendary Pokémon [Groudon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groudon "Groudon") to dry up the oceans of Hoenn and increase the region's landmass; in _Sapphire_, Team Aqua are the villains and they try to use Groudon's counterpart, [Kyogre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyogre "Kyogre"), to flood the landmasses of Hoenn and increase the region's ocean.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-22) Prior to facing the eighth Gym Leader, the player has a showdown with Magma or Aqua where the team's leader uses a mystical orb that awakens the slumbering Pokémon, believing it has the power to enthrall their respective target, only for the Pokémon to become enraged and cause catastrophic, region-wide climate changes—a drought in _Ruby_, and heavy rainfall in _Sapphire_—until it is defeated or captured by the protagonist.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-23) The player's father Norman also introduces them to Wally, a sickly young boy whom the player helps capture a Pokémon to be his companion as he moves away from the big city. Wally eventually overcomes his illness and becomes a successful Pokémon Trainer, ultimately becoming the final challenger the player must face before the Elite Four.

## Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Development")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/JunichiMasudaJI1.jpg/250px-JunichiMasudaJI1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JunichiMasudaJI1.jpg)

Development director Junichi Masuda

_Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ were developed by [Game Freak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Freak "Game Freak") and [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") under the direction of [Junichi Masuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junichi_Masuda "Junichi Masuda"). As with its predecessors, [Ken Sugimori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Sugimori "Ken Sugimori") was the art director, although these were the first games in which he did not single-handedly produce all of the art.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-24) When asked where his design team came up with the ideas for all of the new Pokémon, Sugimori stated that they got their ideas from past experiences in their childhood involving nature, animals, and the media and then base them on insects. Even looking at the world in a different perspective sometimes provided inspiration for the creatures. "First we select an insect and after that we add essential elements to the insects to make it more like Pokemon, such as adding some hard shape to it, to be more like steel," Sugimori said, describing the process of creating a Pokémon.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-interview-25)

As the Game Boy Advance was able to handle enhanced graphics, _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ were the first games in the series that allowed up to four people to share information at one time, as opposed to the previous limit of two. However, the development team used a more basic graphics engine to keep the game simple and not overly confusing. The team wanted the games to appeal to a large audience, so the game was designed to be easy enough for younger generations of children to play, but new features were added to bring the veteran gamers back.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-interview-25)

Masuda stated that the basic philosophy of all _Pokémon_ games is communication; in the _Pokémon_ series, this is manifested in trading and battling with other people. When asked about the new concept of [double battles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gameplay_of_Pok%C3%A9mon#Double_battles "Gameplay of Pokémon"), the developers noted that they tried to focus more on the original one-on-one battles as the main type of competition and only added the double battles as a "new challenge". They stated that if they receive positive feedback about the double battles, the feature may appear more in future generations.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-interview-25)

The games were the first in the series that did not contain all of the Pokémon from previous generations. Sugimori stated that the team tried to include all the new Pokémon as well as some from previous generations. When asked about any features that could not be included due to technical restrictions, Masuda noted that he wanted each individual Pokémon to make up to three different cries depending on its mood.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-interview-25)

The audio of _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ consists entirely of game music and sound effects; all dialogue is on-screen. The music, composed by Junichi Masuda, Go Ichinose and Morikazu Aoki, is completely instrumental except for two tracks with vocals, "Trick Master" and "Slateport City". The soundtrack of the game was released under the Mediafactory label in Japan on April 26, 2003; the album reached #297 on the [Oricon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oricon "Oricon") charts and charted for one week.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-26) Junichi Masuda wrote only battle tunes, Go Ichinose wrote most of the town, route, fanfare & 'Spotted' tunes, whereas Morikazu Aoki did the remainder.

The soundtrack is noted for its heavy use of [trumpets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trumpet "Trumpet"),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-27) but it also makes heavy use of French horns, strings ensembles, and even pianos.

## Release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Release")]

_Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ were released in Japan on November 21, 2002,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-releasedates-28) in North America on March 19, 2003,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-29) in Australia on April 3, 2003,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-30)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-releasedates-28) and in Europe on July 25, 2003.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-releasedates-28) Nintendo did not promote _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ at [E3 2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2002 "E3 2002");[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-31)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-32) however, it launched a US$ $7 million promotional campaign that lasted from March to May 2003.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-Tobi-33) In July and August 2002 they were promoted through a tour across Japan at Pokémon Festa 2002.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-34) In addition to rewarding pre-orders of the games with merchandise, Nintendo held a contest in which participants submitted videos of themselves singing the [_Pokémon_ theme song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Theme "Pokémon Theme") with their own re-written lyrics; the grand prize for that event was a [Lugia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lugia "Lugia")[PT Cruiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PT_Cruiser "PT Cruiser").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-35)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-36) Later that year, Nintendo launched the EON Ticket Summer Tour, in which 125 [Toys "R" Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toys_%22R%22_Us "Toys \"R\" Us") stores across the United States offered the Eon Ticket e-Card in stores from July 19 to September 1.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-eonticket-15)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-37) Nintendo aired two [television advertisements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_advertisement "Television advertisement"), "Faces" and "Names", on prime-time network, cable, and syndication. "Faces" featured Pokémon juxtaposed with human look-alikes; "Names" featured people shouting out the names of Pokémon and emphasized the fact that the games introduced 100 new Pokémon.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-Tobi-33) Additionally, Nintendo collaborated with United Kingdom beverage brand [Vimto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vimto "Vimto") to promote the games.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-38)

### _Pokémon Emerald_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Pokémon Emerald")]

Main article: [_Pokémon Emerald_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Emerald "Pokémon Emerald")

_**Pokémon Emerald Version**_[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-39) is a third version after _Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_, developed by Game Freak, published by The Pokémon Company and Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance. It was first released in Japan in 2004, and was later released internationally in 2005.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-40)_Emerald_ received generally positive reception[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-41) and by fiscal year 2007 sales had reached 6.32 million units.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-42)
