The games were met with mostly positive reviews. _[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")_ gave them an "Amazing" 9.5 out of 10 rating and awarded them the Editor's Choice Award; in 2007, the games were collectively named the tenth best Game Boy Advance game of all time in an _IGN_ article.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-54)_GameZone_ also gave the games a 9.5 out of 10 rating and awarded them an Outstanding Award.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamezone-52)_[GamePro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GamePro "GamePro")_ gave the games 5 out of 5 stars and named them Editor's Choices.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamepro-55)_[ComputerAndVideoGames.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ComputerAndVideoGames.com "ComputerAndVideoGames.com")_ gave the games a 9 out of 10, and _[GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot "GameSpot")_ gave the games 8.1 out of 10,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-cavrev-48) naming it the best Game Boy Advance game of March 2003.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gotm-56)_[Eurogamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurogamer "Eurogamer")_ and _[1UP.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1UP.com "1UP.com")_ were less enthusiastic about the games, however; _Eurogamer_ gave the games 7 out of 10, and _1UP.com_ gave them a B−.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-1up-47)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-euro-49)

Reviewers were divided in their critiques of the games, especially concerning the gameplay and graphics. _IGN_ praised the "deep design" and noted that the addition of features such as double battles greatly increased the strategic aspect of the games. _GamePro_ also thought that the addition of double battles "add[ed] challenge" and "made the harder battles far more strategic than before—the way the game should be".[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamepro-55) Likewise, _ComputerAndVideoGames.com_ called the gameplay "incredibly compelling and addictive".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-cavrev-48)_GameZone_ noted that the gameplay was more refined and challenging than that of previous titles.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamezone-52) However, _GameSpot_ called the games "a cakewalk from start to finish" and claimed that _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ "don't offer much of a challenge".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamespot-51)_Eurogamer_ also felt that the mechanics "[get] very tired, very fast".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-euro-49)_1UP.com_ also felt that the games were formulaic and that double battles were underused.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-1up-47)

_ComputerAndVideoGames.com_ was enthusiastic over the graphics, calling them "gorgeous".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-cavrev-48) Other reviewers were less enthusiastic, however. _GamePro_ felt that the graphics were only "a fair bit prettier" than those of the Game Boy Color games;[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamepro-55)_GameZone_ said that the games "still [use] the simple animations and basic character designs that were created for the original, color-less Game Boy".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamezone-52)_IGN_ and _1UP.com_ noted that the graphics had received only a minor upgrade,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-1up-47)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-IGNp3-57) and _Eurogamer_ felt that the graphics had been upgraded to a "functional level at best".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-euro-49) The audio was generally well-received: _GameZone_ and _GameSpot_ both felt the audio was catchy; _GameZone_ gave the audio an 8 out of 10 score, saying that while the music "was annoying at times, [...] it's also very good. [...] I found myself humming the music when I wasn't playing". Other complaints included the removal of the time system of _Gold_ and _Silver_ and the inability to import Pokémon from the games of previous generations.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-IGNp3-57)

### Sales

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Sales")]

_Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ were highly anticipated.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-58)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-59) In Japan, they sold 1.25 million units within the first four days of release and were the best-selling games of the 2002 holiday season;[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-60) sales totaled around 4.4 million within six weeks of release.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-NMM-61) They also became the first games to sell 2 million copies in Japan since 2001's _[Final Fantasy X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final\_Fantasy\_X "Final Fantasy X")_ and the first games for a handheld console to do so since 2000's _Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Monsters 4_.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-62)[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-63)

In North America, Nintendo sold 2.2 million units by April 2003, less than one month after the games' release in that region.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-NMM-61) In the United States, _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ were the second- and third-best-selling games of 2003, respectively.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-64)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-65)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-66) The games enjoyed success in Europe as well.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-67) Even before release, European retailers imported cartridges from the United States to meet the high demand.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-68)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-69) Upon release, 500,000 copies were sold in its first weekend and sold 1.5 million within eight weeks.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-70)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-71) They were the second-best-selling games of the holiday season in 2002.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-72) The games were brought up at [E3 2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2003 "E3 2003") by [Satoru Iwata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoru_Iwata "Satoru Iwata") as a symbol of how successful the Game Boy Advance was at the time.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-73)

With 16.22 million units sold worldwide as of 2023, they are the [best-selling games for the Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_Game_Boy_Advance_video_games "List of best-selling Game Boy Advance video games").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-74)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-75) However, analysts noted that with "young kids...gravitating toward _[Yu-Gi-Oh!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yu-Gi-Oh! "Yu-Gi-Oh!")_" at the time, _Pokémon_'s popularity was waning even before the American release of _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-76)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-77)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-78)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-79)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-80) This was reflected in the games' sales compared to those of previous generations: [_Red_ and _Blue_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Red_and_Blue "Pokémon Red and Blue") sold nearly 31 million units worldwide,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-81) and [_Gold_ and _Silver_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Gold_and_Silver "Pokémon Gold and Silver") sold over 23 million units.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-82)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-83)

## Legacy

Main article: [_Pokémon Omega Ruby_ and _Alpha Sapphire_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Omega_Ruby_and_Alpha_Sapphire "Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire")

_**Pokémon Omega Ruby**_[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-84) and _**Pokémon Alpha Sapphire**_[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-85) are [enhanced remakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_remake "Enhanced remake") of _Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_. The new titles were developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo for the [Nintendo 3DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_3DS "Nintendo 3DS"). They were released worldwide for the [Nintendo 3DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_3DS "Nintendo 3DS") on November 21, 2014, exactly twelve years after the original release date of _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_, while the European release was the following week.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-86)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-87)

#### _Pokémon Box: Ruby and Sapphire_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Pokémon Box: Ruby and Sapphire")]

_**Pokémon Box: Ruby and Sapphire**_[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-88) or simply _**Pokémon Box**_[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-89), is a [spin-off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin-off_(media) "Spin-off (media)")_Pokémon_ game for the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube"), bundled with a [GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube_%E2%80%93_Game_Boy_Advance_link_cable "GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable") and a [Memory Card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_Card "Memory Card") 59.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-ignboxpreview-90) It was released in Japan on May 30, 2003, and in North America on July 12, 2004,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-91) but only through the [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City")[Pokémon Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Center "Pokémon Center") and its online store,[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-ignboxpreview-90) and it is no longer available in either location.[_[as of?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] The game was released in some parts of Europe as _**Pokémon Memory Magic**_ due to translation problems[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-92) and Europeans could only get the game by using points from Nintendo of Europe's loyalty program or by buying the _Pokémon Colosseum Mega Pack_.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-93)

The game is essentially a storage system for the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance")_Pokémon_ games that allow players to trade and store Pokémon that they have caught in _Ruby_, _Sapphire_, _[Emerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Emerald "Pokémon Emerald")_, [_FireRed_ and _LeafGreen_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_FireRed_and_LeafGreen "Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen") onto a GameCube memory card.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-94)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-95) Players can then organize and interact with their Pokémon on the GameCube, such as allowing them to breed. Unique Pokémon can also be acquired. Another feature allows _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ to be played on the television via the GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable. Options such as taking [screenshots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenshot "Screenshot") of the game are available in this mode.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-96) Another addition is the "Showcase", where players can create and display game pieces of Pokémon.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-ignboxreview-97)

Nintendo referred to the game as "the most exclusive Pokémon software ever offered to North American _Pokémon_ fans,"[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-BoxAllgame-98) but it was generally considered to be unnecessary, receiving a score of 50% on [GameRankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameRankings "GameRankings") from 1 review.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-99) Craig Harris of _IGN_ gave the game a "[Meh](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/meh "wiktionary:meh")" rating of 5.0 out of 10, praising the interface, which makes the organization of Pokémon much easier as compared to the Game Boy Advance interface, as well as the emulator which allows _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ to be played on the GameCube. He also stated that the game was a good deal due to the inclusion of a memory card and link cable. However, Harris cited the "Showcase" as "entirely unnecessary and completely out of place", and said that overall the game lacked much to do. He wrote, "It's targeted specifically for the truly die-hard _Pokemon_ fan, but it requires so many specific elements to actually be useful to anyone."[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-ignboxreview-97)_[Allgame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allgame "Allgame")_ gave the game three and a half out of five stars.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-BoxAllgame-98)

_**Pokémon Ruby Version**_[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-1) and _**Pokémon Sapphire Version**_[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-2) are 2002[role-playing video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Role-playing_video_game "Role-playing video game") developed by [Game Freak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Freak "Game Freak") and published by [The Pokémon Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pok%C3%A9mon_Company "The Pokémon Company") and [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") for the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance"). They are the first installments in the third generation of the [_Pokémon_ video game series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_(video_game_series) "Pokémon (video game series)"), also known as the "advanced generation". After years of Nintendo being the sole publisher of the franchise in all regions, The Pokémon Company co-published the games for the first time since the establishment of the joint-owned company in 1998. They were first released in Japan in late 2002, and internationally in 2003. _[Pokémon Emerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Emerald "Pokémon Emerald")_, a third version, was released two years later in each region. [Remakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_remake "Video game remake") of the two games, titled [_Pokémon Omega Ruby_ and _Alpha Sapphire_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Omega_Ruby_and_Alpha_Sapphire "Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire"), were released for the [Nintendo 3DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_3DS "Nintendo 3DS") worldwide in November 2014, exactly twelve years to the date of the original _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ release date, with the exception of Europe, where it released a week later.

The gameplay is mostly unchanged from the previous games; the player controls the main character from an [overhead perspective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhead_perspective "Overhead perspective"), and the controls are largely the same as those of previous games. As with previous games, the main objectives are to catch all of the Pokémon in the games and defeat the [Elite Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elite_Four "Elite Four") and the Pokémon League Champion; also like their predecessors, the games' main subplot involves the player character defeating a criminal organization that attempts to take over the region. New features, such as double battles, [Pokémon abilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_abilities "Pokémon abilities"), Pokémon Contests, and 135 new Pokémon were added.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-3)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-4)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-5) Owing to the increased capabilities of the Game Boy Advance, four players may be [connected to each other](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance_Game_Link_Cable "Game Boy Advance Game Link Cable") at a time instead of the previous limit of two. Additionally, the games can be connected to an [e-Reader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_e-Reader "Nintendo e-Reader") or other third-generation _Pokémon_ games.

_Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ received mostly positive reviews; praise was given to the new features and Pokémon designs, though critics were divided in their assessment of the games, especially on the gameplay and graphics. Most of the complaints focused on gameplay not changing much in relation to previous generations. With over 16.22 million copies sold, they were a commercial success and became the [best-selling game for the Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_Game_Boy_Advance_video_games "List of best-selling Game Boy Advance video games"); however, the games sold less than previous generations with _Red_ and _Blue_ having sold nearly 31 million units worldwide, and _Gold_ and _Silver_ selling over 23.10 million units.

## Gameplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Gameplay")]

See also: [Gameplay of _Pokémon_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gameplay_of_Pok%C3%A9mon "Gameplay of Pokémon")

The basic mechanics of _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ are largely the same as their predecessors. As with all _Pokémon_ games for [handheld consoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handheld_console "Handheld console"), the gameplay is in [third-person](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third-person_(video_games) "Third-person (video games)"), overhead perspective and consists of three basic screens: a [field map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overworld "Overworld"), in which the player navigates the main character; a battle screen; and the menu, in which the player configures their party, items, or gameplay settings. Players begin the game with one Pokémon and can capture more using [Poké Balls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9_Ball "Poké Ball"). They can also use their Pokémon to battle other Pokémon. When the player [encounters a wild Pokémon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_encounter "Random encounter") or is challenged by a trainer to a battle, the screen switches to a [turn-based](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn-based "Turn-based") battle screen where the Pokémon fight.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-6) During a battle, the player may [use a move](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gameplay_of_Pok%C3%A9mon#Pok%C3%A9mon_moves "Gameplay of Pokémon"), use an item, switch their active Pokémon, or flee, although fleeing is not an option in battles against trainers. All Pokémon have [hit points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hit_points "Hit points") (HP); when a Pokémon's HP is reduced to zero, it faints and cannot battle until it is revived. If the player's Pokémon defeats the opposing Pokémon (causes it to faint), it receives [experience points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_points "Experience points"). After accumulating enough experience points, it will [level up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_point#Level-based_progression "Experience point"); most Pokémon [evolve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_evolution "Pokémon evolution") into a new species of Pokémon when they reach a certain level.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-7)

Apart from battling, capturing Pokémon is the most essential element of _Pokémon_ gameplay. During a battle with a wild Pokémon, the player may use a Poké Ball on them. If successful, the Pokémon will be added to the player's active party, or stored if the player already has the maximum six Pokémon in their party.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-8) Factors in the success rate of capture include the HP, status effects such as Paralysis or Sleep, and the strength of the Poké Ball used: the lower the target's HP and the stronger the Poké Ball, the higher the success rate of capture is.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-9) Other trainers' Pokémon cannot be captured.

### New features

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: New features")]

See also: [List of generation III Pokémon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_generation_III_Pok%C3%A9mon "List of generation III Pokémon")

The most prominent change in the battle mechanics is the introduction of double battles, in which the opposing parties each use two Pokémon at the same time. Consequently, certain [Pokémon moves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_moves "Pokémon moves") can affect multiple combatants at once.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-10) Multi battles were added alongside double battles. They are identical to double battles, but there are two trainers to a side, each controlling one of the two Pokémon sent out. Also new to the games are [innate abilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_abilities "Pokémon abilities") and [natures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_natures "Pokémon natures"); the former is shared by every Pokémon of a certain species, while the latter may vary among a particular species. Abilities grant their holders certain powers in battle, such as immunity against certain [types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_types "Pokémon types") of moves or strengthening a certain type of move. Natures, like innate abilities, affect the strength of Pokémon in battle; however, they affect the stats of the Pokémon rather than directly affecting the strength of the moves.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-11) Another stat introduced in _Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ is Condition, an important factor in Pokémon Contests, mini-games in which participants perform moves before a judge. Both Pokémon and their moves have a Condition, which is increased by using Pokéblocks, which are candies made from berries.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-12) Secret bases were added as a one-off feature where players could open up a hole in the world and customize the area with various items picked up in-game. Players who linked up with others who set up secret bases were able to battle an [NPC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-player_character "Non-player character") version of that trainer within their secret base.

Like [_Pokémon Gold_, _Silver_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Gold_and_Silver "Pokémon Gold and Silver"), and _[Crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Crystal "Pokémon Crystal")_, _Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ keep track of real-life time; this influences events like tides and berry plant growth. However, unlike their predecessors, _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ do not differentiate between day and night. Also, due to the differences in the technical specifications of Game Boy link cables and Game Boy Advance link cables, _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ cannot be linked with Pokémon games of previous generations; one cannot battle with or trade with the previous generations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-13)

### Connectivity to other devices

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Connectivity to other devices")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Eon_Ticket.jpg/250px-Eon_Ticket.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eon_Ticket.jpg)

The Eon Ticket could be scanned in by the [e-Reader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_e-Reader "Nintendo e-Reader") to go and catch either [Latios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latios "Latios") or [Latias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latias "Latias"), depending on the game.

_Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ have limited [e-Reader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_e-Reader "Nintendo e-Reader") support. Nintendo released Battle-e Cards, a set of e-Reader cards that contained trainer battles in which the player could see previously hidden Pokémon.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-14) A special e-Reader card called the Eon Ticket was also released; obtained through the Mystery Gift function, the Ticket allows the player to reach a place called Southern Island. There, the player faces either [Latios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latios "Latios") or [Latias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latias "Latias"), depending on which version of the game is used.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-eonticket-15)

_Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ are also able to connect to the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube") games _[Pokémon Colosseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Colosseum "Pokémon Colosseum")_, _[Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_XD:\_Gale\_of\_Darkness "Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness")_ and _[Pokémon Box: Ruby and Sapphire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Box:\_Ruby\_and\_Sapphire "Pokémon Box: Ruby and Sapphire")_. In the former two, once players reach a certain point in the game, they are able to transfer Pokémon between _Colosseum_ / _XD_ and _Ruby_ / _Sapphire_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-16) Additionally, those who pre-ordered _Colosseum_ were able to access the Pokémon [Jirachi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jirachi "Jirachi") and see a preview of the movie _[Pokémon: Jirachi Wish Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon:\_Jirachi\_Wish\_Maker "Pokémon: Jirachi Wish Maker")_. _Pokémon Box_ allows players to store and organize their Pokémon on the GameCube.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-17) Also, in the European version of _[Pokémon Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Channel "Pokémon Channel")_, players could receive a Jirachi at a certain point in the game, which they could then transfer over to _Ruby_ or _Sapphire_.

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Plot")]

### Setting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Setting")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/7/75/Hoenn_%28map%29.jpg/250px-Hoenn_%28map%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hoenn_(map).jpg)

_Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ are set in the Hoenn Region, designed to be similar to Japan's island of Kyushu if rotated 90°. (pictured below).

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Kyushu_relief_map.svg/250px-Kyushu_relief_map.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kyushu_relief_map.svg)

[Kyushu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyushu "Kyushu") island, Japan

_Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ occur in the Hoenn Region, some distance from the Kanto and Johto Regions featured in previous games. The design of Hoenn was based on the Japanese island and region of [Kyushu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyushu "Kyushu"); however, Hoenn is rotated 90° relative to Kyushu, as [Junichi Masuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junichi_Masuda "Junichi Masuda") felt that it would provide a better gameplay balance.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-hiddenpower-18) Like Kyushu, Hoenn possesses many smaller islands, and part of the region is dominated by sea routes, several of which contain areas where the player can dive underwater.

### Story

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Story")]

See also: [List of _Pokémon_ characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pok%C3%A9mon_characters "List of Pokémon characters") and [List of Pokémon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pok%C3%A9mon "List of Pokémon")

Like other _Pokémon_ games, _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_'s gameplay is [linear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_gameplay "Linear gameplay"); the main events occur in a fixed order.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-19) The [protagonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protagonist "Protagonist") of _Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ are Brendan and May, who have recently moved to a small town called Littleroot Town. At the beginning of the games, the player chooses either [Treecko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treecko "Treecko"), [Torchic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torchic "Torchic"), or [Mudkip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudkip "Mudkip") to protect Professor Birch, the regional professor, from attacking [Poochyena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poochyena "Poochyena"). After defending Birch, the player is taken to his lab and receives the chosen Pokémon as their [starter Pokémon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starter_Pok%C3%A9mon "Starter Pokémon"). After that, the player encounters May/Brendan, the child of Professor Birch. The player's rival, who appears as the professor's child, is also a [Pokémon Trainer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Trainer "Pokémon Trainer") and occasionally battles the player.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-20) The games' two main goals are defeating the eight Gym Leaders, proving oneself worthy of challenging the Elite Four and Hoenn League Champion to become the new Hoenn League Champion and completing the [Pokédex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9dex "Pokédex") by capturing, evolving, and trading to obtain all 202 Pokémon available between _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_. It is possible to obtain all 386 Pokémon, but this requires trading with [_Pokémon FireRed_ and _LeafGreen_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_FireRed_and_LeafGreen "Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen") or _[Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_XD:\_Gale\_of\_Darkness "Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness")_ and _[Pokémon Colosseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Colosseum "Pokémon Colosseum")_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-21)

In addition to the main quest of defeating the Gym Leaders, there are side quests in which the player can aid NPCs by fulfilling tasks, usually by obtaining items. The most prominent subplot involves [Team Aqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_Aqua "Team Aqua") and [Team Magma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_Magma "Team Magma"), crime syndicates who want to use Pokémon to alter the climate of Hoenn: in _Ruby_, the villains, Team Magma, want to use the legendary Pokémon [Groudon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groudon "Groudon") to dry up the oceans of Hoenn and increase the region's landmass; in _Sapphire_, Team Aqua are the villains and they try to use Groudon's counterpart, [Kyogre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyogre "Kyogre"), to flood the landmasses of Hoenn and increase the region's ocean.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-22) Prior to facing the eighth Gym Leader, the player has a showdown with Magma or Aqua where the team's leader uses a mystical orb that awakens the slumbering Pokémon, believing it has the power to enthrall their respective target, only for the Pokémon to become enraged and cause catastrophic, region-wide climate changes—a drought in _Ruby_, and heavy rainfall in _Sapphire_—until it is defeated or captured by the protagonist.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-23) The player's father Norman also introduces them to Wally, a sickly young boy whom the player helps capture a Pokémon to be his companion as he moves away from the big city. Wally eventually overcomes his illness and becomes a successful Pokémon Trainer, ultimately becoming the final challenger the player must face before the Elite Four.

## Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Development")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/JunichiMasudaJI1.jpg/250px-JunichiMasudaJI1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JunichiMasudaJI1.jpg)

Development director Junichi Masuda

_Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ were developed by [Game Freak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Freak "Game Freak") and [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo "Nintendo") under the direction of [Junichi Masuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junichi_Masuda "Junichi Masuda"). As with its predecessors, [Ken Sugimori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Sugimori "Ken Sugimori") was the art director, although these were the first games in which he did not single-handedly produce all of the art.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-24) When asked where his design team came up with the ideas for all of the new Pokémon, Sugimori stated that they got their ideas from past experiences in their childhood involving nature, animals, and the media and then base them on insects. Even looking at the world in a different perspective sometimes provided inspiration for the creatures. "First we select an insect and after that we add essential elements to the insects to make it more like Pokemon, such as adding some hard shape to it, to be more like steel," Sugimori said, describing the process of creating a Pokémon.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-interview-25)

As the Game Boy Advance was able to handle enhanced graphics, _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ were the first games in the series that allowed up to four people to share information at one time, as opposed to the previous limit of two. However, the development team used a more basic graphics engine to keep the game simple and not overly confusing. The team wanted the games to appeal to a large audience, so the game was designed to be easy enough for younger generations of children to play, but new features were added to bring the veteran gamers back.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-interview-25)

Masuda stated that the basic philosophy of all _Pokémon_ games is communication; in the _Pokémon_ series, this is manifested in trading and battling with other people. When asked about the new concept of [double battles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gameplay_of_Pok%C3%A9mon#Double_battles "Gameplay of Pokémon"), the developers noted that they tried to focus more on the original one-on-one battles as the main type of competition and only added the double battles as a "new challenge". They stated that if they receive positive feedback about the double battles, the feature may appear more in future generations.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-interview-25)

The games were the first in the series that did not contain all of the Pokémon from previous generations. Sugimori stated that the team tried to include all the new Pokémon as well as some from previous generations. When asked about any features that could not be included due to technical restrictions, Masuda noted that he wanted each individual Pokémon to make up to three different cries depending on its mood.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-interview-25)

The audio of _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ consists entirely of game music and sound effects; all dialogue is on-screen. The music, composed by Junichi Masuda, Go Ichinose and Morikazu Aoki, is completely instrumental except for two tracks with vocals, "Trick Master" and "Slateport City". The soundtrack of the game was released under the Mediafactory label in Japan on April 26, 2003; the album reached #297 on the [Oricon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oricon "Oricon") charts and charted for one week.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-26) Junichi Masuda wrote only battle tunes, Go Ichinose wrote most of the town, route, fanfare & 'Spotted' tunes, whereas Morikazu Aoki did the remainder.

The soundtrack is noted for its heavy use of [trumpets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trumpet "Trumpet"),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-27) but it also makes heavy use of French horns, strings ensembles, and even pianos.

## Release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Release")]

_Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ were released in Japan on November 21, 2002,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-releasedates-28) in North America on March 19, 2003,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-29) in Australia on April 3, 2003,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-30)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-releasedates-28) and in Europe on July 25, 2003.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-releasedates-28) Nintendo did not promote _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ at [E3 2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2002 "E3 2002");[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-31)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-32) however, it launched a US$ $7 million promotional campaign that lasted from March to May 2003.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-Tobi-33) In July and August 2002 they were promoted through a tour across Japan at Pokémon Festa 2002.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-34) In addition to rewarding pre-orders of the games with merchandise, Nintendo held a contest in which participants submitted videos of themselves singing the [_Pokémon_ theme song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Theme "Pokémon Theme") with their own re-written lyrics; the grand prize for that event was a [Lugia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lugia "Lugia")[PT Cruiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PT_Cruiser "PT Cruiser").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-35)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-36) Later that year, Nintendo launched the EON Ticket Summer Tour, in which 125 [Toys "R" Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toys_%22R%22_Us "Toys \"R\" Us") stores across the United States offered the Eon Ticket e-Card in stores from July 19 to September 1.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-eonticket-15)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-37) Nintendo aired two [television advertisements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_advertisement "Television advertisement"), "Faces" and "Names", on prime-time network, cable, and syndication. "Faces" featured Pokémon juxtaposed with human look-alikes; "Names" featured people shouting out the names of Pokémon and emphasized the fact that the games introduced 100 new Pokémon.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-Tobi-33) Additionally, Nintendo collaborated with United Kingdom beverage brand [Vimto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vimto "Vimto") to promote the games.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-38)

### _Pokémon Emerald_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Pokémon Emerald")]

Main article: [_Pokémon Emerald_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Emerald "Pokémon Emerald")

_**Pokémon Emerald Version**_[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-39) is a third version after _Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_, developed by Game Freak, published by The Pokémon Company and Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance. It was first released in Japan in 2004, and was later released internationally in 2005.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-40)_Emerald_ received generally positive reception[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-41) and by fiscal year 2007 sales had reached 6.32 million units.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-42)

The games were met with mostly positive reviews. _[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN")_ gave them an "Amazing" 9.5 out of 10 rating and awarded them the Editor's Choice Award; in 2007, the games were collectively named the tenth best Game Boy Advance game of all time in an _IGN_ article.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-54)_GameZone_ also gave the games a 9.5 out of 10 rating and awarded them an Outstanding Award.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamezone-52)_[GamePro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GamePro "GamePro")_ gave the games 5 out of 5 stars and named them Editor's Choices.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamepro-55)_[ComputerAndVideoGames.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ComputerAndVideoGames.com "ComputerAndVideoGames.com")_ gave the games a 9 out of 10, and _[GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot "GameSpot")_ gave the games 8.1 out of 10,[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-cavrev-48) naming it the best Game Boy Advance game of March 2003.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gotm-56)_[Eurogamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurogamer "Eurogamer")_ and _[1UP.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1UP.com "1UP.com")_ were less enthusiastic about the games, however; _Eurogamer_ gave the games 7 out of 10, and _1UP.com_ gave them a B−.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-1up-47)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-euro-49)

Reviewers were divided in their critiques of the games, especially concerning the gameplay and graphics. _IGN_ praised the "deep design" and noted that the addition of features such as double battles greatly increased the strategic aspect of the games. _GamePro_ also thought that the addition of double battles "add[ed] challenge" and "made the harder battles far more strategic than before—the way the game should be".[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamepro-55) Likewise, _ComputerAndVideoGames.com_ called the gameplay "incredibly compelling and addictive".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-cavrev-48)_GameZone_ noted that the gameplay was more refined and challenging than that of previous titles.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamezone-52) However, _GameSpot_ called the games "a cakewalk from start to finish" and claimed that _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ "don't offer much of a challenge".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamespot-51)_Eurogamer_ also felt that the mechanics "[get] very tired, very fast".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-euro-49)_1UP.com_ also felt that the games were formulaic and that double battles were underused.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-1up-47)

_ComputerAndVideoGames.com_ was enthusiastic over the graphics, calling them "gorgeous".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-cavrev-48) Other reviewers were less enthusiastic, however. _GamePro_ felt that the graphics were only "a fair bit prettier" than those of the Game Boy Color games;[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamepro-55)_GameZone_ said that the games "still [use] the simple animations and basic character designs that were created for the original, color-less Game Boy".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-gamezone-52)_IGN_ and _1UP.com_ noted that the graphics had received only a minor upgrade,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-1up-47)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-IGNp3-57) and _Eurogamer_ felt that the graphics had been upgraded to a "functional level at best".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-euro-49) The audio was generally well-received: _GameZone_ and _GameSpot_ both felt the audio was catchy; _GameZone_ gave the audio an 8 out of 10 score, saying that while the music "was annoying at times, [...] it's also very good. [...] I found myself humming the music when I wasn't playing". Other complaints included the removal of the time system of _Gold_ and _Silver_ and the inability to import Pokémon from the games of previous generations.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-IGNp3-57)

### Sales

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Sales")]

_Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ were highly anticipated.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-58)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-59) In Japan, they sold 1.25 million units within the first four days of release and were the best-selling games of the 2002 holiday season;[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-60) sales totaled around 4.4 million within six weeks of release.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-NMM-61) They also became the first games to sell 2 million copies in Japan since 2001's _[Final Fantasy X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final\_Fantasy\_X "Final Fantasy X")_ and the first games for a handheld console to do so since 2000's _Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Monsters 4_.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-62)[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-63)

In North America, Nintendo sold 2.2 million units by April 2003, less than one month after the games' release in that region.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-NMM-61) In the United States, _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ were the second- and third-best-selling games of 2003, respectively.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-64)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-65)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-66) The games enjoyed success in Europe as well.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-67) Even before release, European retailers imported cartridges from the United States to meet the high demand.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-68)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-69) Upon release, 500,000 copies were sold in its first weekend and sold 1.5 million within eight weeks.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-70)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-71) They were the second-best-selling games of the holiday season in 2002.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-72) The games were brought up at [E3 2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2003 "E3 2003") by [Satoru Iwata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satoru_Iwata "Satoru Iwata") as a symbol of how successful the Game Boy Advance was at the time.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-73)

With 16.22 million units sold worldwide as of 2023, they are the [best-selling games for the Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_Game_Boy_Advance_video_games "List of best-selling Game Boy Advance video games").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-74)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-75) However, analysts noted that with "young kids...gravitating toward _[Yu-Gi-Oh!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yu-Gi-Oh! "Yu-Gi-Oh!")_" at the time, _Pokémon_'s popularity was waning even before the American release of _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-76)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-77)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-78)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-79)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-80) This was reflected in the games' sales compared to those of previous generations: [_Red_ and _Blue_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Red_and_Blue "Pokémon Red and Blue") sold nearly 31 million units worldwide,[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-81) and [_Gold_ and _Silver_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Gold_and_Silver "Pokémon Gold and Silver") sold over 23 million units.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-82)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-83)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Remakes")]

Main article: [_Pokémon Omega Ruby_ and _Alpha Sapphire_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Omega_Ruby_and_Alpha_Sapphire "Pokémon Omega Ruby and Alpha Sapphire")

_**Pokémon Omega Ruby**_[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-84) and _**Pokémon Alpha Sapphire**_[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-85) are [enhanced remakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_remake "Enhanced remake") of _Pokémon Ruby_ and _Sapphire_. The new titles were developed by Game Freak and published by Nintendo for the [Nintendo 3DS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_3DS "Nintendo 3DS"). #### _Pokémon Box: Ruby and Sapphire_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pok%C3%A9mon_Ruby_and_Sapphire&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Pokémon Box: Ruby and Sapphire")]

_**Pokémon Box: Ruby and Sapphire**_[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-88) or simply _**Pokémon Box**_[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-89), is a [spin-off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin-off_(media) "Spin-off (media)")_Pokémon_ game for the [GameCube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube "GameCube"), bundled with a [GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameCube_%E2%80%93_Game_Boy_Advance_link_cable "GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable") and a [Memory Card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_Card "Memory Card") 59.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-ignboxpreview-90) It was released in Japan on May 30, 2003, and in North America on July 12, 2004,[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-91) but only through the [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City")[Pokémon Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Center "Pokémon Center") and its online store,[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-ignboxpreview-90) and it is no longer available in either location.[_[as of?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] The game was released in some parts of Europe as _**Pokémon Memory Magic**_ due to translation problems[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-92) and Europeans could only get the game by using points from Nintendo of Europe's loyalty program or by buying the _Pokémon Colosseum Mega Pack_.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-93)

The game is essentially a storage system for the [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance "Game Boy Advance")_Pokémon_ games that allow players to trade and store Pokémon that they have caught in _Ruby_, _Sapphire_, _[Emerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon\_Emerald "Pokémon Emerald")_, [_FireRed_ and _LeafGreen_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_FireRed_and_LeafGreen "Pokémon FireRed and LeafGreen") onto a GameCube memory card.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-94)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-95) Players can then organize and interact with their Pokémon on the GameCube, such as allowing them to breed. Unique Pokémon can also be acquired. Another feature allows _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ to be played on the television via the GameCube – Game Boy Advance link cable. Options such as taking [screenshots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenshot "Screenshot") of the game are available in this mode.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-96) Another addition is the "Showcase", where players can create and display game pieces of Pokémon.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-ignboxreview-97)

Nintendo referred to the game as "the most exclusive Pokémon software ever offered to North American _Pokémon_ fans,"[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-BoxAllgame-98) but it was generally considered to be unnecessary, receiving a score of 50% on [GameRankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameRankings "GameRankings") from 1 review.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-99) Craig Harris of _IGN_ gave the game a "[Meh](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/meh "wiktionary:meh")" rating of 5.0 out of 10, praising the interface, which makes the organization of Pokémon much easier as compared to the Game Boy Advance interface, as well as the emulator which allows _Ruby_ and _Sapphire_ to be played on the GameCube. He also stated that the game was a good deal due to the inclusion of a memory card and link cable. However, Harris cited the "Showcase" as "entirely unnecessary and completely out of place", and said that overall the game lacked much to do. He wrote, "It's targeted specifically for the truly die-hard _Pokemon_ fan, but it requires so many specific elements to actually be useful to anyone."[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-ignboxreview-97)_[Allgame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allgame "Allgame")_ gave the game three and a half out of five stars.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pok%C3%A9mon_Box:_Ruby_and_Sapphire#cite_note-BoxAllgame-98)
